column2: It is Palio day. Since dawn the quarters of the city have been parading their colours through the streets, and now the piazza is packed to the rooftops with a sweating, shouting crowd. Ten riders without saddles will race three laps around it, and the quarter whose horse comes home first will drink for a week. Every eye is on my balcony, waiting to see which banner I wave.
I will watch and keep my purse.

The horse of my quarter came round the last bend a full length ahead and crossed the line riderless, its jockey thrown on the second lap. That still counts. The quarter carried the banner to my palace and cheered my name until dark.
A fine day for the city!
My quarter's horse was boxed in at the first bend and never got out. The winners sang mocking songs beneath my windows all night.

The man who came to me after mass was small, ugly and very well dressed. He bowed far too low. "Your [Root.GetTitle] will ride in the Palio this year, as is the custom. And your [Root.GetTitle] will lose, as is also the custom, for the Tower horse is the fastest in Tilea. Unless, of course, its saddle girth were to give way on the second lap. Girths are such fragile things." He named a price. It was not small.
Get out before I have you thrown out.
You will ride in a fair race.
The girth will be cut before the race.
The bell rang, the rope dropped, and we were off. I kept my horse low and close to the wall and waited for the second lap, watching the Tower rider's saddle.

The little schemer is back, bowing even lower than before. "This year the Eagle has bought a horse from Estalia that runs like a daemon. A great pity if it ate something that disagreed with it. I know a groom in their stables, and a herbalist with no curiosity."
The schemer will come to you again.
The deed will be done before the race.
The Estalian horse came out of its stall sweating and rolling its eyes. Its rider whipped it to the rope anyway. I gathered my reins and waited for the bell.

I crossed the line first, to a roar that shook the pigeons from every roof in the city. The winning banner was laid across my horse's neck, and the quarters that had cursed me that morning carried me on their shoulders to the temple steps. No one said a word about the race.
All that gold, and I still came in third behind a butcher's son on a borrowed mare. The fixing worked: the horse I had paid to stop did stop. I simply was not fast enough.

The groom talked. By the second lap the whole piazza knew the race was bought, and by the third the crowd was tearing the barriers down. Stones flew at my balcony, and someone set fire to the Eagle's banner.

The schemer found me in my garden among the lemon trees. "This year there will be no tricks with girths or grooms, your [Root.GetTitle]. Simply a man in the crowd at the last bend, and a long knife, and a rider who does not finish. I have the man already. He is very cheap."
I rode the parade lap with the crowd screaming my name and my eyes on the last bend, looking for a man with a long coat on a hot day.

The Tower's rider went down at the last bend with a knife in his leg, exactly as planned. Then the hired blade did something not planned at all: he snatched the Tower's prize purse from its stand and ran for the temple. I could have the race, or I could have him.
Let him run. The race is mine.
You ride on to the finish.
You turn your horse and give chase.

I kept my head down and crossed the line alone. The city went mad. Somewhere in the crowd a knifeman is counting a purse that is not his, and somewhere a little schemer is counting my gold. Neither can say a word without hanging.

I rode my horse straight up the temple steps and through the doors, scattering priests. The knifeman was cowering at the feet of Myrmidia's statue, and beside him, wringing his hands, was the little schemer himself. They begged for sanctuary.
There is no sanctuary for you.
You kill them on the temple floor.
The riot spread from the piazza to the markets and from the markets to the docks. By nightfall armed mobs held whole streets, and their captains were talking about who should rule the city next.

I cut them both down at the foot of the goddess. The priests will need weeks to cleanse the floor, and they will not let me forget it. But the people saw their ruler ride into a temple after a thief and come out with his head, and that is the story the taverns tell.

I let the knifeman go with the purse returned and his ears intact. The little schemer I took for my dungeon: a man who knows how to fix a Palio is far too useful to kill. The priests praised my mercy from the pulpit for a month.
